## Proof

We evaluate
$$L = \lim_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g\!\left(\frac{x}{h}\right) f(x)\,dx.$$

**Step 1: Change of variables.** Set $u = x/h$, so $x = hu$ and $dx = h\,du$. Since $g(x/h)=0$ whenever $|x/h|\ge 1$, i.e. $|x|\ge |h|$, the integrand is supported on $[-|h|,|h|]$, so the change of variables is valid over all of $\mathbb{R}$.

For $h>0$: as $x$ ranges over $\mathbb{R}$, $u$ ranges over $\mathbb{R}$, and
$$\frac{1}{h}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g\!\left(\frac{x}{h}\right) f(x)\,dx = \frac{1}{h}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(u)\,f(hu)\,h\,du = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(u)\,f(hu)\,du.$$

For $h<0$: writing $h=-|h|$, as $x$ goes from $-\infty$ to $+\infty$, $u=x/h$ goes from $+\infty$ to $-\infty$, so
$$\frac{1}{h}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g\!\left(\frac{x}{h}\right) f(x)\,dx = \frac{1}{h}\int_{+\infty}^{-\infty} g(u)\,f(hu)\,h\,du = \frac{1}{h}\cdot h\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(u)\,f(hu)\,du = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(u)\,f(hu)\,du.$$

In both cases the expression reduces to
$$I(h) := \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(u)\,f(hu)\,du.$$

**Step 2: Reduce to a compact interval.** Since $g(u)=0$ for $|u|\ge 1$,
$$I(h) = \int_{-1}^{1} g(u)\,f(hu)\,du.$$

**Step 3: Take the limit.** Because $f$ is continuous at $0$, for every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists $\delta>0$ such that $|y|<\delta \Rightarrow |f(y)-f(0)|<\varepsilon$. For $|h|<\delta$ (noting $|u|\le 1$ so $|hu|\le |h|<\delta$), we have $|f(hu)-f(0)|<\varepsilon$ for all $u\in[-1,1]$. Therefore
$$\left|I(h)-f(0)\right| = \left|\int_{-1}^{1} g(u)\bigl(f(hu)-f(0)\bigr)\,du\right| \le \varepsilon\int_{-1}^{1} g(u)\,du = \varepsilon\cdot 1 = \varepsilon,$$
where we used $g\ge 0$ and $\int g = 1$.

Since $\varepsilon>0$ was arbitrary,
$$\lim_{h\to 0} I(h) = f(0).$$

**Conclusion.** The two one-sided limits agree, so
$$\boxed{\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{1}{h} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g\!\left(\frac{x}{h}\right) f(x)\,dx = f(0).}$$
